Private control plane vs customer-managed control plane
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-24 15:00 PDT | Duration: ~59 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Andrew Ross (Veridian Head of Security), Priya Menon (Veridian Cloud Architect), Samir Gupta (CTO), Ellen Park (Compliance)

[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. This is Maya from Redwood, Liam's here as our solutions engineer. Quick round robin?
[00:12] Andrew Ross: Andrew Ross, head of security at Veridian. We'll mostly be focused on private deployment and the compliance questions.
[00:18] Priya Menon: Priya, cloud architect — I'll own the network and ops questions.
[00:22] Samir Gupta: Samir, CTO, here to understand impacts to latency and integration with our services.
[00:27] Ellen Park: Ellen, compliance manager, SOC 2 lead.
[00:30] Liam Chen: Liam Chen, SE at Redwood — I'll walk through the architecture and network details.

[01:05] Maya: Great. Agenda: quick overview of the Private VPC model, then Liam to deep dive on network isolation, ingress/egress, firewalling, KMS and audit logs, then Q&A and next steps. We'll drop links to docs in the chat.

[02:10] Liam Chen: Okay starting high level: Redwood Private runs a customer-dedicated control plane in your VPC; compute nodes (the inference fleet) can be in customer-managed subnets or in an on-prem rack. We support three patterns: 1) VPC-hosted with peered subnets, 2) VPC with AWS PrivateLink to Redwood control plane, or 3) fully on-prem air-gapped. We'll focus on (1) and (2) today since Veridian is cloud-first.

[03:05] Priya: Quick clarification — when you say "control plane in our VPC" do you mean we run the Kubernetes/control services, or Redwood manages it but it's logically isolated?

[03:18] Liam: Good question. Two modes: customer-managed control plane where you deploy our control plane container images into your VPC/K8s cluster (you own networking, IAM, and KMS keys); or Redwood-managed private control plane that is deployed in a customer-dedicated account with strict network peering and private connectivity — in that mode Redwood operates the control plane but never has public internet egress to your data. We often recommend customer-managed for high-regulation shops.

[04:10] Andrew: For Veridian we prefer the customer-managed control plane to keep keys and audit within our control.

[04:22] Liam: Perfect. In that model, keys live in your KMS (we support AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and external HSM via PKCS#11). Encryption at rest uses envelope encryption; Redwood stores only ciphertext.

[04:45] Ellen: How do you handle key rotation and access — do Redwood service accounts ever get access to plaintext?

[04:53] Liam: No plaintext access. The runtime requests decryption through your KMS via short-lived credentials. We support per-tenant keys and an audit trail for each decrypt request. Key rotation is supported — we recommend a rewrap workflow where new keys are used to re-encrypt metadata; we have tooling to assist. We'll share the rewrap runbook.

[06:00] [06:00] Priya: Network — talk us through ingress. We need to restrict inbound only from our app gateways and limit egress heavily.

[06:10] Liam: For inbound (ingress) we expect requests to hit your API gateway which then connects to the inference fleet over private subnets. If you use VPC peering or Transit Gateway, you can lock the inference subnets so only specific CIDR ranges and security groups can reach the nodes. We recommend using an application layer proxy (NLB + ALB) with mutual TLS to authenticate calls.

[07:05] Maya: Note: some customers instead front Redwood endpoints with an internal API proxy that performs token exchange and RBAC enforcement — that pattern reduces attack surface and centralizes auth.

[08:00] Andrew: Egress is our bigger concern — we can't allow the inference nodes to reach the public internet except for very specific destinations (KMS, internal telemetry collector). How does Redwood support egress restrictions?

[08:15] Liam: You can put NAT gateways behind strict route tables and proxy logic. We ship a small sidecar that handles outbound calls and can be configured to only allow traffic to whitelisted hostnames/IPs. For control plane operations that require package updates we support an offline package bundle or an internal artifact repository.

[09:00] Priya: Does the sidecar perform DNS filtering? We use internal DNS to resolve and allow only FQDNs in our allowlist.

[09:10] Liam: Yes, sidecar allows FQDN-based allowlists; it also supports TLS interception with customer-provided certs if you need deeper inspection — though that has compliance implications. Most customers use mTLS+IP whitelists + egress proxy for telemetry/SIEM forwarding.

[10:20] [10:20] Samir: Latency question: adding a sidecar/proxy — impact on tail latency for inference? We're very sensitive.

[10:30] Liam: We measured <5ms additional median latency on NVLink-backed GPUs for single-token calls when sidecar is used for egress; for heavy batching the impact amortizes. We'll share the benchmark spreadsheet. If you need sub-10ms p99 constraints, we can recommend colocating the proxy in the same host namespace and tuning batch sizes.

[11:45] Ellen: Audit logs — we need full fidelity for decrypt ops, admin actions, and model changes. What does Redwood provide out of box?

[12:00] Liam: Redwood emits structured JSON audit logs for all control-plane actions: deployments, rollouts, model pulls, key decrypt requests, and admin API calls. Logs can be forwarded to your SIEM via CloudWatch/Stackdriver or directly to an S3 bucket. Logs include request IDs, user/service principal, and IP/subnet origin. We also support immutable log storage via S3 with Object Lock for compliance.

[13:25] Andrew: Can we get logs with the exact KMS key ID and operation?

[13:30] Liam: Yes — decrypt attempts include KMS key ID, envelope key metadata, and operation result. We redact prompt content by default but keep metadata. If you need prompt retention for QA we offer opt-in with stricter access controls.

[14:40] [14:40] Priya: Firewall rules — show us an example rule set for the inference subnet.

[14:50] Liam: Example: allow inbound from app gateway SG on TCP 443 to inference nodes; deny 0.0.0.0/0 inbound; egress to KMS endpoints (AWS KMS regional IPs or PrivateLink), egress to S3 endpoints for model artifacts (use VPC endpoints), egress to your telemetry collector IP range; block all other egress. We'll attach a sample Terraform snippet in the notes.

[16:05] Maya: We'll also include a sample security group and NACL baseline — remember NACLs are stateless so we prefer security groups + route table restrictions.

[17:20] [17:20] Andrew: On the control plane side — if Redwood operates it in a customer-dedicated account, what network paths exist back to Redwood? We need to ensure no unintended peering exists.

[17:32] Liam: In that mode we only use private endpoints — PrivateLink or SSH bastion via customer-approved IPs. There's no default route to Redwood's management plane; everything goes over mutually authenticated private connections that you control. We also support periodic IP allowlisting for Redwood operator access.

[18:45] Ellen: For SOC 2 evidence, can you provide the architecture diagrams, encryption KPI, and a list of admin accounts with 2FA enforcement?

[18:58] Maya: Yes — we'll send our SOC 2 pack which includes architecture, controls matrix, incident response runbook, and sample admin audit logs. Note that when the control plane is customer-managed, those artifacts are split: Redwood provides the software controls, you provide evidence of configuration and operator access.

[20:10] Priya: On-prem air-gapped: we have one data center where we might want to host inference; what does that install look like?

[20:22] Liam: We provide an on-prem bundle — container images, an offline artifact repo, and an install script. We recommend a hardened bastion for admin access, strict firewall rules, and an internal artifact mirror for models. KMS integration in air-gapped mode requires an HSM on-prem or an offline key transfer process. It's more manual but supported.

[22:00] [22:00] Samir: Anything we should watch for with model updates and CVEs — how do you handle patching?

[22:10] Liam: We publish CVE advisories for runtime components. For customer-managed installs you control update cadence; Redwood provides signed bundles and a recommended patching schedule. For critical patches we provide an emergency patch bundle and guidance.

[24:05] Andrew: Incident response — how quickly can your team rotate keys or revoke access if suspicious activity is detected?

[24:18] Liam: Key revoke is immediate if you disable the KMS key; any subsequent decrypts will fail. For access revocation in Redwood-managed modes we can disable service principals and rotate service credentials; for customer-managed you control IAM and can revoke in minutes. We also support certificate revocation lists for mTLS between proxies.

[26:00] [26:00] Ellen: For compliance, we need proof of regular access reviews. Do you provide automated reports of admin access and role changes?

[26:12] Liam: Yes, audit logs include role change events and admin API calls. We can generate periodic CSV reports of user role assignments and recent admin activity for auditors.

[28:40] Priya: About egress to S3 for model pulls — we want to restrict via VPC endpoint only. Does Redwood support S3 VPC endpoints and IAM role-based access for model fetch?

[28:55] Liam: Absolutely. We recommend model artifact stores in your account and using IAM roles for cross-account fetch when needed. Use VPC endpoints and bucket policies to lock down access.

[30:00] [30:00] Maya: Quick product note: Redwood Optimize and the server runtime will cache embeddings and KV cache — caching is local to the inference nodes and encrypted. Cache eviction and lifetime are configurable.

[31:20] Andrew: Is the cache encrypted with the same KMS keys?

[31:28] Liam: Yes, cache blobs are envelope encrypted with your KMS keys before being persisted. Access patterns are logged.

[33:00] [33:00] Samir: Let's talk about RBAC and SSO integration — we use Okta. Can Redwood tie into our SSO and map Okta groups to roles?

[33:12] Liam: We support SAML and OIDC. You can map Okta groups to Redwood roles via SSO claims; we also support SCIM for user provisioning. Admin actions require 2FA and we can enforce device posture via your IdP.

[34:45] Ellen: Can we restrict who can view prompts/outputs? We need separation between model ops and product analytics.

[34:56] Liam: Role-based policies allow restricting access to prompt view. We redact prompt content by default; viewing prompts requires a specific role and audit logging. We'll show the role matrix in the deck.

[36:10] [36:10] Priya: Anything special for Firewalling between GPUs and management plane?

[36:20] Liam: Management plane traffic is control-plane RPCs on pinned ports — restrict it to the control-plane subnets and allow only specific SGs. Use private IPs, no public endpoints. For host-level protection we recommend host-based firewalls + CIS benchmarks.

[38:05] Andrew: We have a compliance requirement for data residency — all model inference data must stay in our EU region. Can Redwood guarantee region affinity?

[38:16] Maya: Yes, for customer-managed deployments you deploy in your EU region. For Redwood-managed private we can restrict scheduling to specific regions and provide data residency contracts. We'll add language to the agreement.

[40:00] [40:00] Samir: What about secrets — do you allow secretless deployments where credentials never touch disk?

[40:12] Liam: We support in-memory secrets; credential helper fetches short-lived tokens at runtime and doesn't persist them. If you need FIPS/HSM, we support FIPS-compliant builds and HSM-backed keys.

[42:30] Ellen: Auditors will want a runbook for model updates and data handling. Do you have a sample runbook?

[42:40] Maya: Yes we'll include a sample in the SOC 2 pack and a change management checklist. It outlines who approves model rollout, test thresholds, smoke tests, and rollback steps.

[44:00] Priya: Any gotchas when integrating with Transit Gateway and multiple VPCs?

[44:11] Liam: Route propagation can expose unintended networks — we recommend explicit route tables and using prefix lists. Also be mindful of overlapping CIDRs. We can help review your TGW policy.

[46:20] [46:20] Andrew: Competitor question — how are you different from the large public providers like Anthropic/AWS in private deployments?

[46:30] Maya: Key differences: we provide inference-optimized runtime with control over batching/quantization, strong observability geared for unit economics, and flexible deployment modes. We focus on production SLAs and cost controls that big public stacks don't expose to this level.

[48:00] Liam: Also our private deployment is built for customer-managed keys and private networking as a first-class flow — not an afterthought.

[49:10] Priya: Okay next steps and timelines — Priya will send our network diagram, Redwood will return the SOC pack and Terraform samples, and we aim to kick off a pilot mid-April.

[49:25] Maya: Confirming: pilot target start 2026-04-12, 2-week run, Redwood provides benchmark scripts.

[50:00] Ellen: We'll need the SOC 2 docs before our internal compliance meeting on 2026-04-02.

[50:10] Maya: Noted — send by 2026-03-31.

[51:00] [51:00] Closing Q&A — small clarifications on logging format and sample command lines for KMS rewrap. Liam shared a quick snippet in chat.

[52:20] Andrew: One last thing — can we do a short security review with your engineering lead next week? Technical deep dive on our network config with Liam and your infra lead.

[52:35] Maya: Yes we'll set that up; I'll include Redwood infra lead and schedule for the week of 2026-03-29.

[54:00] [54:00] The call winds down, attendees exchange pleasantries.

[55:20] Priya: Thanks everyone — we appreciate the detail.

[55:30] Samir: Thanks, very helpful.

[55:35] Liam: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the artifacts.

[58:45] Maya: End. Links shared: SOC2_pack.pdf (link), terraform-sg-examples.tf (link), benchmark-spreadsheet.xlsx (link).

Transcript notes: occasional mis-transcriptions present; some proper nouns (e.g., PrivateLink IPs) generalized for redaction.
